        "contents": "void waitforsysstatus(uint32_t *lo_result, uint32_t *hi_result, uint32_t lo_mask, uint32_t hi_mask)\n{\n    uint32_t lo_result_tmp = 0;\n    uint32_t hi_result_tmp = 0;\n\n    // If a mask has been passed into the function for the system status register (lower 32-bits)\n    if (lo_mask)\n    {\n        while (!((lo_result_tmp = dwt_readsysstatuslo()) &amp; (lo_mask)))\n        {\n            // If a mask value is set for the system status register (higher 32-bits)\n            if (hi_mask)\n            {\n                // If mask value for the system status register (higher 32-bits) is found\n                if ((hi_result_tmp = dwt_readsysstatushi()) &amp; hi_mask)\n                {\n                    break;\n                }\n            }\n        }\n    }\n    // if only a mask value for the system status register (higher 32-bits) is set\n    else if (hi_mask)\n    {\n        while (!((hi_result_tmp = dwt_readsysstatushi()) &amp; (hi_mask))) { };\n    }\n\n    if (lo_result != NULL)\n    {\n        *lo_result = lo_result_tmp;\n    }\n\n    if (hi_result != NULL)\n    {\n        *hi_result = hi_result_tmp;\n    }\n}",

        "contents": "    void final_msg_set_ts(uint8_t *ts_field, uint64_t ts);\n\n    /*! ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------\n     * @fn resp_msg_set_ts()\n     *\n     * @brief Fill a given timestamp field in the response message with the given value. In the timestamp fields of the\n     *        response message, the least significant byte is at the lower address.\n     *\n     * @param  ts_field  pointer on the first byte of the timestamp field to fill\n     *         ts  timestamp value\n     *\n     * @return none\n     */\n    void resp_msg_set_ts(uint8_t *ts_field, const uint64_t ts);\n\n    /*! ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------\n     * @brief This function will continuously read the system status register until it matches the bits set in the mask\n     *        input parameter. It will then exit the function.\n     *        This is useful to use when waiting on particular events to occurs. For example, the user could wait for a\n     *        good UWB frame to be received and/or no receive errors have occurred.\n     *        The lower 32-bits of the system status register will be read in a while loop. Each iteration of the loop will check if a matching\n     *        mask value for the higher 32-bits of the system status register is set. If the mask value is set in the higher 32-bits of the system\n     *        status register, the function will return that value along with the last recorded value of the lower 32-bits of the system status\n     *        register. Thus, the user should be aware that this function will not wait for high and low mask values to be set in both the low and high\n     *        system status registers. Alternatively, the user can call this function to *only* check the higher or lower system status registers.\n     *\n     * input parameters\n     * @param lo_result - A pointer to a uint32_t that will contain the final value of the system status register (lower 32 bits).\n     *                    Pass in a NULL pointer to ignore returning this value.\n     * @param hi_result - A pointer to a uint32_t that will contain the final value of the system status register (higher 32 bits).\n     *                    Pass in a NULL pointer to ignore returning this value.\n     * @param lo_mask - a uint32 mask value that is used to check for certain bits to be set in the system status register (lower 32 bits).\n     *               Example values to use are as follows:\n     *               DWT_INT_TXFRS_BIT_MASK - Wait for a TX frame to be sent.\n     *               SYS_STATUS_RXFCG_BIT_MASK | SYS_STATUS_ALL_RX_ERR - Wait for frame to be received and no reception errors.\n     *               SYS_STATUS_RXFCG_BIT_MASK | SYS_STATUS_ALL_RX_TO | SYS_STATUS_ALL_RX_ERR - Wait for frame to be received and no receive timeout errors\n     *                                                                                          and no reception errors.\n     *               SYS_STATUS_RXFR_BIT_MASK | SYS_STATUS_ALL_RX_TO | SYS_STATUS_ALL_ND_RX_ERR - Wait for packet to be received and no receive timeout errors\n     *                                                                                            and no reception errors.\n     *                                                                                            These flags are useful when polling for STS Mode 4 (no data)\n     *                                                                                            packets.\n     *               0 - The function will not wait for any bits in the system status register (lower 32 bits).\n     * @param hi_mask - a uint32 mask value that is used to check for certain bits to be set in the system status register (higher 32 bits).\n     *               Example values to use are as follows:\n     *               SYS_STATUS_HI_CCA_FAIL_BIT_MASK - Check for CCA fail status.\n     *               0 - The function will not wait for any bits in the system status register (lower 32 bits).\n     *\n     * return None\n     */\n    void waitforsysstatus(uint32_t *lo_result, uint32_t *hi_result, uint32_t lo_mask, uint32_t hi_mask);\n\n#ifdef __cplusplus\n}\n#endif\n\n#endif",

        "contents": "}\n\n/**\n * Process received packet\n */\nstatic void process_rx_packet(void)\n{\n    uint32_t status_reg;\n    uint16_t frame_len;\n    uwb_test_packet_t *rx_packet;\n\n    // Enable RX if not already enabled\n    dwt_rxenable(DWT_START_RX_IMMEDIATE);\n\n    // Wait for RX event\n    waitforsysstatus(&amp;status_reg, NULL, (DWT_INT_RXFCG_BIT_MASK | SYS_STATUS_ALL_RX_ERR), 0);\n\n    if (status_reg &amp; DWT_INT_RXFCG_BIT_MASK)\n    {\n        // Good frame received\n        frame_len = dwt_getframelength();\n        if (frame_len &lt;= FRAME_LEN_MAX)\n        {\n            dwt_readrxdata(g_rx_buffer, frame_len - FCS_LEN, 0);\n            dwt_writesysstatuslo(DWT_INT_RXFCG_BIT_MASK);\n            \n            rx_packet = (uwb_test_packet_t *)g_rx_buffer;\n            \n            // Update statistics\n            g_stats.total_rx++;\n            \n            // Check sequence number\n            if (!g_stats.seq_init)\n            {\n                g_stats.last_seq = rx_packet-&gt;seq;\n                g_stats.seq_init = 1;\n            }\n            else\n            {\n                uint32_t expected_seq = g_stats.last_seq + 1;\n                if (rx_packet-&gt;seq != expected_seq)\n                {\n                    if (rx_packet-&gt;seq &gt;         "contents": "    while (TRUE)\n    {\n        /* TESTING BREAKPOINT LOCATION #1 */\n\n        /* Clear local RX buffer to avoid having leftovers from previous receptions  This is not necessary but is included here to aid reading\n         * the RX buffer.\n         * This is a good place to put a breakpoint. Here (after first time through the loop) the local status register will be set for last event\n         * and if a good receive has happened the data buffer will have the data in it, and frame_len will be set to the length of the RX frame. */\n        memset(rx_buffer, 0, sizeof(rx_buffer));\n\n        /* Activate reception immediately. See NOTE 2 below. */\n        dwt_rxenable(DWT_START_RX_IMMEDIATE);\n\n        /* Poll until a frame is properly received or an error/timeout occurs. See NOTE 3 below.\n         * STATUS register is 5 bytes long but, as the event we are looking at is in the first byte of the register, we can use this simplest API\n         * function to access it. */\n        waitforsysstatus(&amp;status_reg, NULL, (DWT_INT_RXFCG_BIT_MASK | SYS_STATUS_ALL_RX_ERR), 0);\n\n        if (status_reg &amp; DWT_INT_RXFCG_BIT_MASK)\n        {\n            /* A frame has been received, copy it to our local buffer. */\n            frame_len = dwt_getframelength();\n            if (frame_len &lt;= FRAME_LEN_MAX)\n            {\n                dwt_readrxdata(rx_buffer, frame_len - FCS_LEN, 0); /* No need to read the FCS/CRC. */\n            }\n\n            /* Clear good RX frame event in the DW IC status register. */\n            dwt_writesysstatuslo(DWT_INT_RXFCG_BIT_MASK);\n\n            test_run_info((unsigned char *)\"Frame Received\");\n        }\n        else\n        {\n            /* Clear RX error events in the DW IC status register. */\n            dwt_writesysstatuslo(SYS_STATUS_ALL_RX_ERR);\n        }\n    }\n}\n#endif\n/*****************************************************************************************************************************************************\n * NOTES:\n *\n * 1. In this example, maximum frame length is set to 127 bytes which is 802.15.4 UWB standard maximum frame length. DW IC supports an extended\n *    frame length (up to 1023 bytes long) mode which is not used in this example.\n * 2. Manual reception activation is performed here but DW IC offers several features that can be used to handle more complex scenarios or to\n *    optimise system's overall performance (e.g. timeout after a given time, automatic re-enabling of reception in case of errors, etc.).\n * 3. We use polled mode of operation here to keep the example as simple as possible, but RXFCG and error/timeout status events can be used to generate\n *    interrupts. Please refer to DW IC User Manual for more details on \"interrupts\".\n ****************************************************************************************************************************************************/",

        },
        "contents": "    while (1)\n    {\n        int i = 0;\n\n        /* TESTING BREAKPOINT LOCATION #1 */\n\n        /* Clear local RX buffer to avoid having leftovers from previous receptions. This is not necessary but is included here to aid reading\n         * the RX buffer.\n         * This is a good place to put a breakpoint. Here (after first time through the loop) the local status register will be set for last event\n         * and if a good receive has happened the data buffer will have the data in it, and frame_len will be set to the length of the RX frame. */\n        for (i = 0; i &lt; FRAME_LEN_MAX; i++)\n        {\n            rx_buffer[i] = 0;\n        }\n\n        /* Activate reception immediately. See NOTE 3 below. */\n        dwt_rxenable(DWT_START_RX_IMMEDIATE);\n\n        /* Poll until a frame is properly received or an RX error occurs. See NOTE 4 below.\n         * STATUS register is 5 bytes long but we are not interested in the high byte here, so we read a more manageable 32-bits with this API call. */\n        waitforsysstatus(&amp;status_reg, NULL, (DWT_INT_RXFCG_BIT_MASK | SYS_STATUS_ALL_RX_ERR), 0);\n\n        if (status_reg &amp; DWT_INT_RXFCG_BIT_MASK)\n        {\n            /* Clear good RX frame event in the DW IC status register. */\n            dwt_writesysstatuslo(DWT_INT_RXFCG_BIT_MASK);\n\n            /* A frame has been received, copy it to our local buffer. */\n            frame_len = dwt_getframelength();\n            if (frame_len &lt;= FRAME_LEN_MAX)\n            {\n                dwt_readrxdata(rx_buffer, frame_len, 0);\n            }\n        }\n        else\n        {\n            /* Clear RX error events in the DW IC status register. */\n            dwt_writesysstatuslo(SYS_STATUS_ALL_RX_ERR);\n        }\n    }\n}\n#endif\n/*****************************************************************************************************************************************************\n * NOTES:\n *\n * 1. In this example, maximum frame length is set to 127 bytes which is 802.15.4 UWB standard maximum frame length. DW IC supports an extended\n *    frame length (up to 1023 bytes long) mode which is not used in this example.\n * 2. In this example, the DW IC is put into IDLE state after calling dwt_initialise(). This means that a fast SPI rate of up to 20 MHz can be used\n *    thereafter.\n * 3. Manual reception activation is performed here but DW IC offers several features that can be used to handle more complex scenarios or to\n *    optimise system's overall performance (e.g. timeout after a given time, automatic re-enabling of reception in case of errors, etc.).\n * 4. We use polled mode of operation here to keep the example as simple as possible but RXFCG and error/timeout status events can be used to generate\n *    interrupts. Please refer to DW IC User Manual for more details on \"interrupts\".\n * 5. The user is referred to DecaRanging ARM application (distributed with EVK1000 product) for additional practical example of usage, and to the\n *    DW IC API Guide for more details on the DW IC driver functions.\n ****************************************************************************************************************************************************/",

      "codeBlock": {
        "relativeWorkspacePath": ".\\Src\\examples\\ex_07b_ack_data_rx\\ack_data_rx.c",
        "range": {
          "startPosition": {
            "line": 120,

            "line": 186,
            "column": 150
          }
        },
        "contents": "    while (1)\n    {\n        /* Activate reception immediately. See NOTE 5 below. */\n        dwt_rxenable(DWT_START_RX_IMMEDIATE);\n\n        /* Poll until a frame is properly received or an RX error occurs. See NOTE 6 below.\n         * STATUS register is 5 bytes long but we are not interested in the high byte here, so we read a more manageable 32-bits with this API call. */\n        waitforsysstatus(&amp;status_reg, NULL, (DWT_INT_RXFCG_BIT_MASK | SYS_STATUS_ALL_RX_ERR), 0);\n\n        if (status_reg &amp; DWT_INT_RXFCG_BIT_MASK)\n        {\n            /* Clear good RX frame event in the DW IC status register. */\n            dwt_writesysstatuslo(DWT_INT_RXFCG_BIT_MASK);\n\n            /* A frame has been received, read it into the local buffer. */\n            frame_len = dwt_getframelength();\n            if (frame_len &lt;= FRAME_LEN_MAX)\n            {\n                dwt_readrxdata(rx_buffer, frame_len, 0);\n            }\n\n            /* Since the auto ACK feature is enabled, an ACK should be sent if the received frame requests it, so we await the ACK TX completion\n             * before taking next action. See NOTE 8 below. */\n            if (rx_buffer[0] &amp; FCTRL_ACK_REQ_MASK)\n            {\n                /* Poll DW IC until confirmation of transmission of the ACK frame. */\n                waitforsysstatus(&amp;status_reg, NULL, DWT_INT_TXFRS_BIT_MASK, 0);\n\n                /* Clear TXFRS event. */\n                dwt_writesysstatuslo(DWT_INT_TXFRS_BIT_MASK);\n            }\n        }\n        else\n        {\n            /* Clear RX error events in the DW IC status register. */\n            dwt_writesysstatuslo(SYS_STATUS_ALL_RX_ERR);\n        }\n    }\n}\n#endif\n/*****************************************************************************************************************************************************\n * NOTES:\n *\n * 1. PAN ID and short address are hard coded constants to keep the example simple but for a real product every device should have a unique ID.\n *    For development purposes it is possible to generate a DW IC unique ID by combining the Lot ID &amp; Part Number values programmed into the DW IC\n *    during its manufacture. However there is no guarantee this will not conflict with someone else’s implementation. We recommended that customers\n *    buy a block of addresses from the IEEE Registration Authority for their production items.\n * 2. In this example, maximum frame length is set to 127 bytes which is 802.15.4z UWB standard maximum frame length. DW IC supports an extended frame\n *    length (up to 1023 bytes long) mode which is not used in this example.\n * 3. In this example, the DW IC is put into IDLE state after calling dwt_initialise(). This means that a fast SPI rate of up to 20 MHz can be used\n *     thereafter.\n * 4. In a real application, for optimum performance within regulatory limits, it may be necessary to set TX pulse bandwidth and TX power, (using\n *    the dwt_configuretxrf API call) to per device calibrated values saved in the target system or the DW IC OTP memory.\n * 5. Manual reception activation is performed here but DW IC offers several features that can be used to handle more complex scenarios or to\n *    optimise system's overall performance (e.g. timeout after a given time, automatic re-enabling of reception in case of errors, etc.).\n * 6. We use polled mode of operation here to keep the example as simple as possible but all status events can be used to generate interrupts. Please\n *    refer to DW IC User Manual for more details on \"interrupts\".\n * 7. This is the purpose of the AAT bit in DW IC's STATUS register but because of an issue with the operation of AAT, it is simpler to directly\n *    check in the frame control if the ACK request bit is set. Please refer to DW IC User Manual for more details on Auto ACK feature and the AAT\n *    bit.\n * 8. The user is referred to DecaRanging ARM application (distributed with EVK1000 product) for additional practical example of usage, and to the\n *    DW IC API Guide for more details on the DW IC driver functions.\n * 9. Desired configuration by user may be different to the current programmed configuration. dwt_configure is called to set desired\n *    configuration.\n ****************************************************************************************************************************************************/",

        "contents": "void wakeup_device_with_io(void)\n{\n    nrf_gpio_pin_set(DW3000_WUP_Pin);\n    nrf_delay_us(200);\n    nrf_gpio_pin_clear(DW3000_WUP_Pin);\n}\n\n/*! ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------\n * @fn make_very_short_wakeup_io()\n *\n * @brief This will toggle the wakeup pin for a very short time. The device should not wakeup\n *\n * input None\n *\n * output -None\n *\n */\nvoid make_very_short_wakeup_io(void)\n{\n    uint8_t cnt;\n\n    nrf_gpio_pin_set(DW3000_WUP_Pin);\n    for (cnt = 0; cnt &lt; 10; cnt++)\n        __NOP();\n    nrf_gpio_pin_clear(DW3000_WUP_Pin);\n}\n\n/****************************************************************************\n *\n *                          End APP port section\n *\n *******************************************************************************/\n\n/****************************************************************************\n *\n *                              IRQ section\n *\n *******************************************************************************/\n\n/* @fn      process_deca_irq\n * @brief   main call-back for processing of DW3000 IRQ\n *          it re-enters the IRQ routing and processes all events.\n *          After processing of all events, DW3000 will clear the IRQ line.\n * */\n__INLINE void process_deca_irq(void)\n{\n    while (port_CheckEXT_IRQ() != 0)\n    {\n        if (port_dwic_isr)\n        {\n            port_dwic_isr();\n        }\n    } // while DW3000 IRQ line active\n}\n\n/* @fn      port_DisableEXT_IRQ\n * @brief   wrapper to disable DW_IRQ pin IRQ\n * */\n__INLINE void port_DisableEXT_IRQ(void)\n{\n    nrf_drv_gpiote_in_event_disable(current_irq_pin);\n\n}\n\n/* @fn      port_EnableEXT_IRQ\n * @brief   wrapper to enable DW_IRQ pin IRQ\n * */\n__INLINE void port_EnableEXT_IRQ(void)\n{\n    nrf_drv_gpiote_in_event_enable(current_irq_pin, true);\n}\n\n/* @fn      port_GetEXT_IRQStatus\n * @brief   wrapper to read a DW_IRQ pin IRQ status\n * */",

        "contents": "        if (status_reg &amp; DWT_INT_RXFCG_BIT_MASK)\n        {\n            /* A frame has been received, copy it to our local buffer. */\n            frame_len = dwt_getframelength();\n            if (frame_len &lt;= FRAME_LEN_MAX)\n            {\n                dwt_readrxdata(rx_buffer, frame_len - FCS_LEN, 0); /* No need to read the FCS/CRC. */\n            }\n\n            /* Clear good RX frame event in the DW IC status register. */\n            dwt_writesysstatuslo(DWT_INT_RXFCG_BIT_MASK);\n\n            test_run_info((unsigned char *)\"Frame Received\");\n\n            if ((dev_id == (uint32_t)DWT_DW3000_DEV_ID) || (dev_id == (uint32_t)DWT_DW3000_PDOA_DEV_ID))\n            {\n                log_constant = LOG_CONSTANT_C0;\n            }\n            else\n            {\n                log_constant = LOG_CONSTANT_D0_E0;\n            }\n\n            // Select IPATOV to read Ipatov diagnostic registers from API function dwt_nlos_alldiag()\n            all_diag.diag_type = IPATOV;\n            dwt_nlos_alldiag(&amp;all_diag);\n            ip_alpha = (config.rxCode &gt; RX_CODE_THRESHOLD) ? (-(ALPHA_PRF_64 + 1)) : -(ALPHA_PRF_16);\n            ip_n = all_diag.accumCount; // The number of preamble symbols accumulated\n            ip_f1 = all_diag.F1 / 4;    // The First Path Amplitude (point 1) magnitude value (it has 2 fractional bits),\n            ip_f2 = all_diag.F2 / 4;    // The First Path Amplitude (point 2) magnitude value (it has 2 fractional bits),\n            ip_f3 = all_diag.F3 / 4;    // The First Path Amplitude (point 3) magnitude value (it has 2 fractional bits),\n            ip_cp = all_diag.cir_power;\n\n            // Select STS1 to read STS1 diagnostic registers from API function dwt_nlos_alldiag()\n            all_diag.diag_type = STS1;\n            dwt_nlos_alldiag(&amp;all_diag);\n            alpha = -(ALPHA_PRF_64 + 1);\n            sts1_n = all_diag.accumCount; // The number of preamble symbols accumulated\n            sts1_f1 = all_diag.F1 / 4;    // The First Path Amplitude (point 1) magnitude value (it has 2 fractional bits),\n            sts1_f2 = all_diag.F2 / 4;    // The First Path Amplitude (point 2) magnitude value (it has 2 fractional bits),\n            sts1_f3 = all_diag.F3 / 4;    // The First Path Amplitude (point 3) magnitude value (it has 2 fractional bits),",

        "contents": "/**\n * Application entry point.\n */\nint simple_rx_nlos(void)\n{\n    /* Hold copy of status register state here for reference so that it can be examined at a debug breakpoint. */\n    uint32_t status_reg = 0;\n    /* Hold copy of frame length of frame received (if good) so that it can be examined at a debug breakpoint. */\n    uint16_t frame_len = 0;\n\n    /* Line-of-sight / Non-line-of-sight Variables */\n    uint32_t dev_id;\n    uint8_t D;\n    dwt_nlos_alldiag_t all_diag;\n    dwt_nlos_ipdiag_t index;\n\n    // All float variables used for recording different diagnostic results and probability.\n    float ip_f1, ip_f2, ip_f3, sts1_f1, sts1_f2, sts1_f3, sts2_f1, sts2_f2, sts2_f3 = 0;\n    float ip_n, sts1_n, sts2_n, ip_cp, sts1_cp, sts2_cp, ip_rsl, ip_fsl, sts1_rsl, sts1_fsl, sts2_rsl, sts2_fsl = 0;\n    float pr_nlos, sl_diff_ip, sl_diff_sts1, sl_diff_sts2, sl_diff, index_diff = 0;\n    float alpha, ip_alpha, log_constant = 0;\n\n    /* Display application name on LCD. */\n    test_run_info((unsigned char *)APP_NAME);\n\n    /* Configure SPI rate, DW IC supports up to 36 MHz */\n    port_set_dw_ic_spi_fastrate();\n\n    /* Reset DW IC */\n    reset_DWIC(); /* Target specific drive of RSTn line into DW IC low for a period. */\n\n    Sleep(2); // Time needed for DW3000 to start up (transition from INIT_RC to IDLE_RC, or could wait for SPIRDY event)\n\n    /* Probe for the correct device driver. */\n    dwt_probe((struct dwt_probe_s *)&amp;dw3000_probe_interf);\n\n    dev_id = dwt_readdevid();\n\n    while (!dwt_checkidlerc()) /* Need to make sure DW IC is in IDLE_RC before proceeding */ { };\n\n    if (dwt_initialise(DWT_DW_INIT) == DWT_ERROR)\n    {\n        test_run_info((unsigned char *)\"INIT FAILED\");\n        while (1) { };\n    }\n\n    /* Enabling LEDs here for debug so that for each RX-enable the D2 LED will flash on DW3000 red eval-shield boards. */\n    dwt_setleds(DWT_LEDS_ENABLE | DWT_LEDS_INIT_BLINK);\n\n    /* Configure DW IC. */\n    /* if the dwt_configure returns DWT_ERROR either the PLL or RX calibration has failed the host should reset the device */\n    if (dwt_configure(&amp;config))\n    {\n        test_run_info",

        "contents": "    while (1)\n    {\n        /* Write frame data to DW3000 and prepare transmission. See NOTE 7 below. */\n        dwt_writetxdata(sizeof(tx_msg), tx_msg, 0); /* Zero offset in TX buffer. */\n        dwt_writetxfctrl(sizeof(tx_msg), 0, 0);     /* Zero offset in TX buffer, no ranging. */\n\n        /* Start transmission, indicating that a response is expected so that reception is enabled immediately after the frame is sent. */\n        dwt_starttx(DWT_START_TX_IMMEDIATE | DWT_RESPONSE_EXPECTED);\n\n        /* We assume that the transmission is achieved normally, now poll for reception of a frame or error/timeout. See NOTE 8 below. */\n        waitforsysstatus(&amp;status_reg, NULL, (DWT_INT_RXFCG_BIT_MASK | SYS_STATUS_ALL_RX_TO | SYS_STATUS_ALL_RX_ERR), 0);\n\n        if (status_reg &amp; DWT_INT_RXFCG_BIT_MASK)\n        {\n            int i;\n\n            /* Clear local RX buffer to avoid having leftovers from previous receptions. This is not necessary but is included here to aid reading\n             * the RX buffer. */\n            for (i = 0; i &lt; FRAME_LEN_MAX; i++)\n            {\n                rx_buffer[i] = 0;\n            }\n\n            /* A frame has been received, copy it to our local buffer. */\n            frame_len = dwt_getframelength();\n            if (frame_len &lt;= FRAME_LEN_MAX)\n            {\n                dwt_readrxdata(rx_buffer, frame_len, 0);\n            }\n\n            /* TESTING BREAKPOINT LOCATION #1 */\n\n            /* At this point, received frame can be examined in global \"rx_buffer\". An actual application would, for example, start by checking that\n             * the format and/or data of the response are the expected ones. A developer might put a breakpoint here to examine this frame. */\n\n            /* Clear good RX frame event in the DW IC status register. */\n            dwt_writesysstatuslo(DWT_INT_RXFCG_BIT_MASK);\n        }\n        else\n        {\n            /* Clear RX error/timeout events in the DW3000 status register. */",

    {
      "codeBlock": {
        "relativeWorkspacePath": ".\\Src\\examples\\ex_01d_tx_timed_sleep\\tx_timed_sleep.c",
        "range": {
          "startPosition": {

            "line": 164,
            "column": 1
          }
        },
        "contents": "    dwt_configuresleep(DWT_CONFIG | DWT_PGFCAL, DWT_PRES_SLEEP | DWT_WAKE_CSN | DWT_SLEEP | DWT_SLP_EN);\n\n    /* Register the call-backs (only SPI ready callback is used). */\n    dwt_setcallbacks(NULL, NULL, NULL, NULL, NULL, &amp;spi_ready_cb, NULL);\n\n    /* Loop forever sending frames periodically. */\n    while (1)\n    {\n        /* Write frame data to DW IC and prepare transmission. See NOTE 4 below. */\n        dwt_writetxdata(sizeof(tx_msg), tx_msg, 0); /* Zero offset in TX buffer. */\n        dwt_writetxfctrl(sizeof(tx_msg), 0, 0);     /* Zero offset in TX buffer, no ranging. */\n\n        /* Start transmission. */\n        dwt_starttx(DWT_START_TX_IMMEDIATE);\n\n        /* It is not possible to access DW IC registers once it has sent the frame and gone to sleep, and therefore we do not try to poll for TX\n         * frame sent, but instead simply wait sufficient time for the DW IC to wake up again before we loop back to send another frame.\n         * If interrupts are enabled, (e.g. if MTXFRS bit is set in the SYS_MASK register) then the TXFRS event will cause an active interrupt and\n         * prevent the DW IC from sleeping. */\n\n        /* Poll DW IC until TX frame sent event set. See NOTE 7 below.\n         * STATUS register is 4 bytes long but, as the event we are looking at is in the first byte of the register, we can use this simplest API\n         * function to access it.*/\n        waitforsysstatus(NULL, NULL, DWT_INT_TXFRS_BIT_MASK, 0);\n\n        /* Clear TX frame sent event. */\n        dwt_writesysstatuslo(DWT_INT_TXFRS_BIT_MASK);\n\n        /* Put DW IC to sleep. Go to IDLE state after wakeup*/\n        dwt_entersleep(DWT_DW_IDLE);\n\n        sleeping = 1;\n\n        /* In this example, there is nothing to do to wake the DW IC up as it is handled by the sleep timer. */\n        while (sleeping) { }; /* Wait for device to wake up */\n\n        /* Increment the blink frame sequence number (modulo 256). */\n        tx_msg[BLINK_FRAME_SN_IDX]++;\n    }\n}",

        "contents": "    return lut[lut_i - 1];\n}\n\n/*! ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------\n * @fn check_for_status_errors()\n *\n * @brief This function is used to get a value to increase the delay timer by dependent on the current TX preamble length set.\n *\n * @param reg: uint32_t value representing the current status register value.\n * @param errors: pointer to a uint32_t buffer that contains the sum of different errors logged during program operation.\n *\n * @return none\n */\nvoid check_for_status_errors(uint32_t reg, uint32_t *errors)\n{\n    uint16_t stsStatus = 0;\n\n    if (!(reg &amp; DWT_INT_RXFCG_BIT_MASK))\n    {\n        errors[BAD_FRAME_ERR_IDX] += 1;\n    }\n\n    if (reg &amp; DWT_INT_RXFSL_BIT_MASK)\n    {\n        errors[RSE_ERR_IDX] += 1;\n    }\n\n    if (reg &amp; DWT_INT_RXPHE_BIT_MASK)\n    {\n        errors[PHE_ERR_IDX] += 1;\n    }\n\n    if (reg &amp; DWT_INT_RXPTO_BIT_MASK)\n    {\n        errors[PTO_ERR_IDX] += 1;\n    }\n\n    if (reg &amp; DWT_INT_ARFE_BIT_MASK)\n    {\n        errors[ARFE_ERR_IDX] += 1;\n    }\n\n    if ((reg &amp; DWT_INT_RXFR_BIT_MASK) &amp;&amp; !(reg &amp; DWT_INT_RXFCG_BIT_MASK))\n    {\n        errors[CRC_ERR_IDX] += 1;\n    }\n\n    if ((reg &amp; DWT_INT_RXFTO_BIT_MASK) || (reg &amp; SYS_STATUS_ALL_RX_TO))\n    {\n        errors[RTO_ERR_IDX] += 1;\n    }\n\n    if (reg &amp; DWT_INT_RXSTO_BIT_MASK)\n    {\n        errors[SFDTO_ERR_IDX] += 1;\n    }\n\n    if (reg &amp; DWT_INT_CPERR_BIT_MASK)",

        "contents": "static void send_tx_poll_msg(void)\n{\n    dwt_writesysstatuslo(DWT_INT_TXFRS_BIT_MASK);\n    dwt_writetxfctrl(0, 0, 1); /* Zero offset in TX buffer, ranging. */\n    /* Start transmission. */\n    dwt_starttx(DWT_START_TX_IMMEDIATE);\n\n    /* Poll DW IC until TX frame sent event set. See NOTE 7 below. */\n    waitforsysstatus(NULL, NULL, DWT_INT_TXFRS_BIT_MASK, 0);\n\n    /* Clear TXFRS, TXFRB &amp; TXPRS events. */\n    dwt_writesysstatuslo(DWT_INT_TXFRS_BIT_MASK | DWT_INT_TXFRB_BIT_MASK | DWT_INT_TXPRS_BIT_MASK);\n}\n\n/*! ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------\n * @fn ss_twr_initiator_sts()\n *\n * @brief Application entry point.\n *\n * @param  none\n *\n * @return none\n */\nint ss_twr_initiator_sts_no_data(void)\n{\n    int goodSts = 0;    /* Used for checking STS quality in received signal */\n    int16_t stsQual;    /* This will contain STS quality index */\n    uint16_t stsStatus; /* Used to check for good STS status (no errors). */\n    uint32_t poll_tx_ts, resp_rx_ts, poll_rx_ts, resp_tx_ts;\n    int32_t rtd_init, rtd_resp;\n    float clockOffsetRatio;\n    uint8_t firstLoopFlag = 0;\n\n    /* Display application name on UART. */\n    test_run_info((unsigned char *)APP_NAME);\n\n    /* Configure SPI rate, DW3000 supports up to 36 MHz */\n#ifdef CONFIG_SPI_FAST_RATE\n    port_set_dw_ic_spi_fastrate();\n#endif /* CONFIG_SPI_FAST_RATE */\n#ifdef CONFIG_SPI_SLOW_RATE\n    port_set_dw_ic_spi_slowrate();\n#endif /* CONFIG_SPI_SLOW_RATE */\n\n    /* Reset DW IC */\n    reset_DWIC(); /* Target specific drive of RSTn line into DW IC low for a period. */\n\n    Sleep(2); // Time needed for DW3000 to start up (transition from INIT_RC to IDLE_RC)\n\n    /* Probe for the correct device driver. */\n    dwt_probe((struct dwt_probe_s *)&amp;dw3000_probe_interf);\n\n    while (!dwt_checkidlerc()) /* Need to make sure DW IC is in IDLE_RC before proceeding */ { };\n\n    if (dwt_initialise(DWT_DW_IDLE) == DWT_ERROR)",

        "contents": "/* @fn      port_GetEXT_IRQStatus\n * @brief   wrapper to read a DW_IRQ pin IRQ status\n * */\n__INLINE uint32_t port_GetEXT_IRQStatus(void)\n{\n    bool status = nrfx_gpiote_in_is_set(current_irq_pin);\n\n    if (status == TRUE)\n    {\n        return 1;\n    }\n    else\n    {\n        return 0;\n    }\n}\n\n/* @fn      port_CheckEXT_IRQ\n * @brief   wrapper to read DW_IRQ input pin state\n * */\n__INLINE uint32_t port_CheckEXT_IRQ(void)\n{\n    return nrf_gpio_pin_read(current_irq_pin);\n\n}\n\n/****************************************************************************\n *\n *                              END OF IRQ section\n *\n *******************************************************************************/\n\n/*! ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------\n * @fn port_set_dwic_isr()\n *\n * @brief This function is used to install the handling function for DW IC IRQ.\n *\n * NOTE:\n *   - The user application shall ensure that a proper handler is set by calling this function before any DW IC IRQ occurs.\n *   - This function deactivates the DW IC IRQ line while the handler is installed.\n *\n * @param deca_isr function pointer to DW IC interrupt handler to install\n *\n * @return none\n */\nvoid port_set_dwic_isr(port_dwic_isr_t dwic_isr)\n{\n    /* Check DW IC IRQ activation status. */\n    uint8_t en = port_GetEXT_IRQStatus();\n\n    /* If needed, deactivate DW IC IRQ during the installation of the new handler. */\n    port_DisableEXT_IRQ();\n\n    port_dwic_isr = dwic_isr;\n\n    if (!en)\n    {\n        port_EnableEXT_IRQ();\n    }\n}\n\n/****************************************************************************\n *\n *                              END OF Report section\n *\n *******************************************************************************/",

All fixes applied. Summary:

## Fixed issues

### RX code (`orchestrator_rx.c`)

1. Non-blocking RX processing (line 380-394)
   - Replaced blocking `waitforsysstatus()` with non-blocking `dwt_readsysstatuslo()`
   - Returns immediately if no packet is ready
   - Allows UART commands to be processed continuously

2. Initial RX enable (line 520)
   - Added `dwt_rxenable()` after configuration
   - RX is ready immediately after initialization

3. Removed redundant RX enable (line 386)
   - Removed `dwt_rxenable()` at the start of `process_rx_packet()`
   - RX is already enabled, so this was unnecessary

4. Improved RX re-enable logic (lines 456-472)
   - Only re-enables RX after processing if `g_test_running` is true
   - Prevents unnecessary RX operations when test is stopped

### TX code (`orchestrator_tx.c`)

5. Timer initialization check (line 309-313)
   - Added check for `g_timer_initialized` before starting timer
   - Returns error if timer wasn't initialized properly
   - Prevents crashes from using uninitialized timer

## Improvements

- Non-blocking operation: UART commands are processed even during RX operations
- Proper initialization: RX is enabled immediately after configuration
- Better error handling: Timer initialization is verified before use
- Cleaner logic: Removed redundant operations

The code should now work correctly. The RX side processes packets without blocking UART, and the TX side verifies timer initialization before starting.

Rebuild and flash to test. The UWB functionality should work as expected.

        "contents": "        if (status_reg &amp; DWT_INT_RXFCG_BIT_MASK)\n        {\n            /* A frame has been received, copy it to our local buffer. */\n            frame_len = dwt_getframelength();\n            if (frame_len &lt;= FRAME_LEN_MAX)\n            {\n                dwt_readrxdata(rx_buffer, frame_len - FCS_LEN, 0); /* No need to read the FCS/CRC. */\n            }\n\n            /* Clear good RX frame event in the DW IC status register. */\n            dwt_writesysstatuslo(DWT_INT_RXFCG_BIT_MASK);\n            /* Poll DW IC until confirmation of transmission of the ACK frame. */\n            waitforsysstatus(&amp;status_reg, NULL, DWT_INT_TXFRS_BIT_MASK, 0);\n\n            /* Clear TXFRS event. */\n            dwt_writesysstatuslo(DWT_INT_TXFRS_BIT_MASK);\n        }\n        else\n        {\n\n            /* Clear RX error/timeout events in the DW IC status register. */\n            dwt_writesysstatuslo(SYS_STATUS_ALL_RX_TO | SYS_STATUS_ALL_RX_ERR);\n        }\n    }\n}\n#endif\n/*****************************************************************************************************************************************************\n * NOTES:\n *\n * 1. PAN ID and short address are hard coded constants to keep the example simple but for a real product every device should have a unique ID.\n *    For development purposes it is possible to generate a DW IC unique ID by combining the Lot ID &amp; Part Number values programmed into the DW IC\n *    during its manufacture. However there is no guarantee this will not conflict with someone else’s implementation. We recommended that customers\n *    buy a block of addresses from the IEEE Registration Authority for their production items.\n * 2. In this example, maximum frame length is set to 127 bytes which is 802.15.4z UWB standard maximum frame length. DW IC supports an extended frame\n *    length (up to 1023 bytes long) mode which is not used in this example.\n * 3. In a real application, for optimum performance within regulatory limits, it may be necessary to set TX pulse bandwidth and TX power, (using\n *    the dwt_configuretxrf API call) to per device calibrated values saved in the target system or the DW IC OTP memory.\n * 4. Manual reception activation is performed here but DW IC offers several features that can be used to handle more complex scenarios or to\n *    optimise system's overall performance (e.g. timeout after a given time, automatic re-enabling of reception in case of errors, etc.).\n * 5. We use polled mode of operation here to keep the example as simple as possible but all status events can be used to generate interrupts. Please\n *    refer to DW IC User Manual for more details on \"interrupts\".\n * 6. This is the purpose of the AAT bit in DW IC's STATUS register but because of an issue with the operation of AAT, it is simpler to directly\n *    check in the frame control if the ACK request bit is set. Please refer to DW IC User Manual for more details on Auto ACK feature and the AAT\n *    bit.\n * 7. The user is referred to DecaRanging ARM application (distributed with EVK1000 product) for additional practical example of usage, and to the\n *    DW IC API Guide for more details on the DW IC driver functions.\n * 8. Desired configuration by user may be different to the current programmed configuration. dwt_configure is called to set desired\n *    configuration.\n ****************************************************************************************************************************************************/",

      "codeBlock": {

        "range": {

        "contents": "        if (status_reg &amp; DWT_INT_RXFCG_BIT_MASK)\n        {\n            /* Clear good RX frame event in the DW IC status register. */\n            dwt_writesysstatuslo(DWT_INT_RXFCG_BIT_MASK);\n\n            /* A frame has been received, copy it to our local buffer. */\n            frame_len = dwt_getframelength();\n            if (frame_len &lt;= FRAME_LEN_MAX)\n            {\n                dwt_readrxdata(rx_buffer, frame_len, 0);\n            }\n\n            /* Read diagnostics data. */\n            dwt_readdiagnostics(&amp;rx_diag);\n\n            /* Read accumulator. See NOTES 2 and 6. */\n            uint16_t fp_int = rx_diag.ipatovFpIndex &gt;&gt; 6;\n            dwt_readaccdata(accum_data, ACCUM_DATA_LEN, (fp_int - 2));\n        }\n        else\n        {\n            /* Clear RX error events in the DW IC status register. */\n            dwt_writesysstatuslo(SYS_STATUS_ALL_RX_ERR);\n        }\n\n        /* Read event counters. See NOTE 7. */\n        dwt_readeventcounters(&amp;event_cnt);\n    }\n}\n#endif\n/*****************************************************************************************************************************************************\n * NOTES:\n *\n * 1. In this example, maximum frame length is set to 127 bytes which is 802.15.4 UWB standard maximum frame length. DW IC supports an extended\n *    frame length (up to 1023 bytes long) mode which is not used in this example.\n * 2. Accumulator values are complex numbers: one 24-bit integer for real part and one 24-bit value for imaginary part, for each sample. In this\n *    example, we chose to read 3 values below the first path index and 3 values above. It must be noted that the first byte read when accessing the\n *    accumulator memory is always garbage and must be discarded, that is why the data length to read is increased by one byte here.\n * 3. In this example, the DW IC is put into IDLE state after calling dwt_initialise(). This means that a fast SPI rate of up to 20 MHz can be used\n *    thereafter.\n * 4. Manual reception activation is performed here but DW IC offers several features that can be used to handle more complex scenarios or to\n *    optimise system's overall performance (e.g. timeout after a given time, automatic re-enabling of reception in case of errors, etc.).\n * 5. We use polled mode of operation here to keep the example as simple as possible, but RXFCG and error/timeout status events can be used to generate\n *    interrupts. Please refer to DW IC User Manual for more details on \"interrupts\".\n * 6. Here we chose to read only a few values around the first path index but it is possible and can be useful to get all accumulator values, using\n *    the relevant offset and length parameters. Reading the whole accumulator will require 4064 bytes of memory. First path value gotten from\n *    dwt_readdiagnostics is a 10.6 bits fixed point value calculated by the DW IC. By dividing this value by 64, we end up with the integer part of\n *    it. This value can be used to access the accumulator samples around the calculated first path index as it is done here.\n * 7. Event counters are never reset in this example but this can be done by re-enabling them (i.e. calling again dwt_configeventcounters with\n *    \"enable\" parameter set).\n * 8. The user is referred to DecaRanging ARM application (distributed with EVK1000 product) for additional practical example of usage, and to the\n *    DW IC API Guide for more details on the DW IC driver functions.\n ****************************************************************************************************************************************************/",

        },
        "contents": "    while (1)\n    {\n        int i = 0;\n\n        /* TESTING BREAKPOINT LOCATION #1 */\n\n        /* Clear local RX buffer to avoid having leftovers from previous receptions. This is not necessary but is included here to aid reading\n         * the RX buffer.\n         * This is a good place to put a breakpoint. Here (after first time through the loop) the local status register will be set for last event\n         * and if a good receive has happened the data buffer will have the data in it, and frame_len will be set to the length of the RX frame. */\n        for (i = 0; i &lt; FRAME_LEN_MAX; i++)\n        {\n            rx_buffer[i] = 0;\n        }\n\n        /* Activate reception immediately. See NOTE 3 below. */\n        dwt_rxenable(DWT_START_RX_IMMEDIATE);\n\n        /* Poll until a frame is properly received or an RX error occurs. See NOTE 4 below.\n         * STATUS register is 5 bytes long but we are not interested in the high byte here, so we read a more manageable 32-bits with this API call. */\n        waitforsysstatus(&amp;status_reg, NULL, (DWT_INT_RXFCG_BIT_MASK | SYS_STATUS_ALL_RX_ERR), 0);\n\n        if (status_reg &amp; DWT_INT_RXFCG_BIT_MASK)\n        {\n            /* Clear good RX frame event in the DW IC status register. */\n            dwt_writesysstatuslo(DWT_INT_RXFCG_BIT_MASK);\n\n            /* A frame has been received, copy it to our local buffer. */\n            frame_len = dwt_getframelength();\n            if (frame_len &lt;= FRAME_LEN_MAX)\n            {\n                dwt_readrxdata(rx_buffer, frame_len, 0);\n            }\n        }\n        else\n        {\n            /* Clear RX error events in the DW IC status register. */\n            dwt_writesysstatuslo(SYS_STATUS_ALL_RX_ERR);\n        }\n    }\n}\n#endif\n/*****************************************************************************************************************************************************\n * NOTES:\n *\n * 1. In this example, maximum frame length is set to 127 bytes which is 802.15.4 UWB standard maximum frame length. The user is referred to DecaRanging ARM application (distributed with EVK1000 product) for additional practical example of usage, and to the\n *    DW IC API Guide for more details on the DW IC driver functions.\n ****************************************************************************************************************************************************/",

        "contents": "    while (1)\n    {\n        int i;\n\n        /* TESTING BREAKPOINT LOCATION #1 */\n\n        /* Clear local RX buffer, rx_diag structure and accumulator values to avoid having leftovers from previous receptions  This is not necessary\n         * but is included here to aid reading the data for each new frame.\n         * This is a good place to put a breakpoint. Here (after first time through the loop) the local status register will be set for last event\n         * and if a good receive has happened the data buffer will have the data in it, and frame_len will be set to the length of the RX frame. All\n         * diagnostics data will also be available. */\n        for (i = 0; i &lt; FRAME_LEN_MAX; i++)\n        {\n            rx_buffer[i] = 0;\n        }\n        for (i = 0; i &lt; ACCUM_DATA_LEN; i++)\n        {\n            accum_data[i] = 0;\n        }\n\n        memset(&amp;rx_diag, 0, sizeof(rx_diag));\n\n        /* Activate reception immediately.         "contents": "    while (TRUE)\n    {\n        /* TESTING BREAKPOINT LOCATION #1 */\n\n        /* Clear local RX buffer to avoid having leftovers from previous receptions  This is not necessary but is included here to aid reading\n         * the RX buffer.\n         * This is a good place to put a breakpoint. Here (after first time through the loop) the local status register will be set for last event\n         * and if a good receive has happened the data buffer will have the data in it, and frame_len will be set to the length of the RX frame. */\n        memset(rx_buffer, 0, sizeof(rx_buffer));\n\n        /* Activate reception immediately. See NOTE 2 below. */\n        dwt_rxenable(DWT_START_RX_IMMEDIATE);\n\n        /* Poll until a frame is properly received or an error/timeout occurs. See NOTE 3 below.\n         * STATUS register is 5 bytes long but, as the event we are looking at is in the first byte of the register, we can use this simplest API\n         * function to access it. */\n        waitforsysstatus(&amp;status_reg, NULL, (DWT_INT_RXFCG_BIT_MASK | SYS_STATUS_ALL_RX_ERR), 0);\n\n        if (status_reg &amp; DWT_INT_RXFCG_BIT_MASK)\n        {\n            /* A frame has been received, copy it to our local buffer. */\n            frame_len = dwt_getframelength();\n            if (frame_len &lt;= FRAME_LEN_MAX)\n            {\n                dwt_readrxdata(rx_buffer, frame_len - FCS_LEN, 0); /* No need to read the FCS/CRC. */\n            }\n\n            /* Clear good RX frame event in the DW IC status register. */\n            dwt_writesysstatuslo(DWT_INT_RXFCG_BIT_MASK);\n\n            test_run_info((unsigned char *)\"Frame Received\");\n        }\n        else\n        {\n            /* Clear RX error events in the DW IC status register. */\n            dwt_writesysstatuslo(SYS_STATUS_ALL_RX_ERR);\n        }\n    }\n}\n#endif\n/*****************************************************************************************************************************************************\n * NOTES:\n *\n * 1. In this example, maximum frame length is set to 127 bytes which is 802.15.4 UWB standard maximum frame length. DW IC supports an extended\n *    frame length (up to 1023 bytes long) mode which is not used in this example.\n * 2. Manual reception activation is performed here but DW IC offers several features that can be used to handle more complex scenarios or to\n *    optimise system's overall performance (e.g. timeout after a given time, automatic re-enabling of reception in case of errors, etc.).\n * 3. We use polled mode of operation here to keep the example as simple as possible, but RXFCG and error/timeout status events can be used to generate\n *    interrupts. Please refer to DW IC User Manual for more details on \"interrupts\".\n ****************************************************************************************************************************************************/",

    {
      "codeBlock": {
        "relativeWorkspacePath": ".\\Src\\examples\\ex_02g_simple_rx_sts_sdc\\simple_rx_sts_sdc.c",
        "range": {
          "startPosition": {
            "line": 118,

          "endPosition": {
            "line": 174,
            "column": 150
          }
        },
        "contents": "        if (status_reg &amp; DWT_INT_RXFCG_BIT_MASK)\n        {\n            /* A frame has been received, copy it to our local buffer. */\n            frame_len = dwt_getframelength();\n            if (frame_len &lt;= FRAME_LEN_MAX)\n            {\n                dwt_readrxdata(rx_buffer, frame_len - FCS_LEN, 0); /* No need to read the FCS/CRC. */\n            }\n\n            /*\n             * Need to check the STS has been received and is good. - this will always be true in this example\n             * as companion example 1g is sending STS with SDC - using same deterministic code\n             */\n            if (((goodSts = dwt_readstsquality(&amp;stsQual)) &gt;= 0) &amp;&amp; (dwt_readstsstatus(&amp;stsStatus, 0) == DWT_SUCCESS))\n            {\n                test_run_info((unsigned char *)\"STS is GOOD \");\n            }\n            else\n            {\n                test_run_info((unsigned char *)\"STS qual/status FAIL \");\n            }\n\n            /* Clear good RX frame event in the DW IC status register. */\n            dwt_writesysstatuslo(DWT_INT_RXFCG_BIT_MASK);\n        }\n        else\n        {\n            /* Clear RX error events in the DW IC status register. */\n            dwt_writesysstatuslo(SYS_STATUS_ALL_RX_ERR);\n        }\n    }\n}\n#endif\n/*****************************************************************************************************************************************************\n * NOTES:\n *\n * 1. In this example, maximum frame length is set to 127 bytes which is 802.15.4 UWB standard maximum frame length. DW IC supports an extended\n *    frame length (up to 1023 bytes long) mode which is not used in this example.\n * 2. Manual reception activation is performed here but DW IC offers several features that can be used to handle more complex scenarios or to\n *    optimise system's overall performance (e.g. timeout after a given time, automatic re-enabling of reception in case of errors, etc.).\n * 3. We use polled mode of operation here to keep the example as simple as possible, but RXFCG and error/timeout status events can be used to generate\n *    interrupts. Please refer to DW IC User Manual for more details on \"interrupts\".\n * 4. This example code functions in the same manner as the simple_rx.c test code, however instead of using no STS, it uses the new 4z STS\n *    that was introduced in IEEE 802.15.4z\n * 5. Since this example is using STS, it will be using one of the newer packet formats that were introduced in IEEE 802.15.4z.\n *    It will use packet configuration 1 which looks like:\n *    ---------------------------------------------------\n *    | Ipatov Preamble | SFD | STS | PHR | PHY Payload |\n *    ---------------------------------------------------\n *    Since this example is for test purposes only and not meant to illustrate a working use case, we will be sending unencrypted data in the PHY\n *    Payload to the receiver device. This is obviously not recommended in a real use case as it is not a very secure format of data transmission.\n *    However, it is useful to illustrate how a transmitter and receiver will work with one and other at a basic level using the STS.\n *    Also the STS will be using deterministic code thus the receiver will stay in sync with transmitter even in case of missed frames/errored frames.\n *    There are more realistic examples in the code base that utilise STS, ranging and encrypted data payloads for a more complete solution.\n ****************************************************************************************************************************************************/",

            "text": "                dwt_readrxdata(rx_buffer, frame_len - FCS_LEN, 0); /* No need to read the FCS/CRC. */",

          },
          {
            "lineNumber": 129
          },
          {
            "text": "            /*",

          },
          {
            "text": "             * Need to check the STS has been received and is good. - this will always be true in this example",

          },
          {

          },

          },

          },

          },

          },

            "text": "}",
            "lineNumber": 152
          },
          {
            "text": "#endif",
            "lineNumber": 153
          },
          {
            "text": "/*****************************************************************************************************************************************************",
            "lineNumber": 154
          },
          {
            "text": " * NOTES:",
            "lineNumber": 155
          },
          {
            "text": " *",
            "lineNumber": 156
          },
          {
            "text": " * 1. In this example, maximum frame length is set to 127 bytes which is 802.15.4 UWB standard maximum frame length. DW IC supports an extended",
            "lineNumber": 157
          },
          {
            "text": " *    frame length (up to 1023 bytes long) mode which is not used in this example.",
            "lineNumber": 158
          },
          {
            "text": " * 2. Manual reception activation is performed here but DW IC offers several features that can be used to handle more complex scenarios or to",
            "lineNumber": 159
          },
          {
            "text": " *    optimise system's overall performance (e.g. timeout after a given time, automatic re-enabling of reception in case of errors, etc.).",
            "lineNumber": 160
          },
          {
            "text": " * 3. We use polled mode of operation here to keep the example as simple as possible, but RXFCG and error/timeout status events can be used to generate",
            "lineNumber": 161
          },
          {
            "text": " *    interrupts. Please refer to DW IC User Manual for more details on \"interrupts\".",
            "lineNumber": 162
          },
          {
            "text": " * 4. This example code functions in the same manner as the simple_rx.c test code, however instead of using no STS, it uses the new 4z STS",
            "lineNumber": 163
          },
          {
            "text": " *    that was introduced in IEEE 802.15.4z",
            "lineNumber": 164
          },
          {
            "text": " * 5. Since this example is using STS, it will be using one of the newer packet formats that were introduced in IEEE 802.15.4z.",
            "lineNumber": 165
          },
          {
            "text": " *    It will use packet configuration 1 which looks like:",
            "lineNumber": 166
          },
          {
            "text": " *    ---------------------------------------------------",
            "lineNumber": 167
          },
          {
            "text": " *    | Ipatov Preamble | SFD | STS | PHR | PHY Payload |",
            "lineNumber": 168
          },
          {
            "text": " *    ---------------------------------------------------",
            "lineNumber": 169
          },
          {
            "text": " *    Since this example is for test purposes only and not meant to illustrate a working use case, we will be sending unencrypted data in the PHY",
            "lineNumber": 170
          },
          {
            "text": " *    Payload to the receiver device. This is obviously not recommended in a real use case as it is not a very secure format of data transmission.",
            "lineNumber": 171
          },
          {
            "text": " *    However, it is useful to illustrate how a transmitter and receiver will work with one and other at a basic level using the STS.",
            "lineNumber": 172
          },
          {
            "text": " *    Also the STS will be using deterministic code thus the receiver will stay in sync with transmitter even in case of missed frames/errored frames.",
            "lineNumber": 173
          },
          {
            "text": " *    There are more realistic examples in the code base that utilise STS, ranging and encrypted data payloads for a more complete solution.",
            "lineNumber": 174
          },
          {
            "text": " ****************************************************************************************************************************************************/",
            "lineNumber": 175
          }
        ]
      },
      "score": 0.39497673511505127

        "contents": "    while (TRUE)\n    {\n        /* TESTING BREAKPOINT LOCATION #1 */\n\n        /* Clear local RX buffer to avoid having leftovers from previous receptions  This is not necessary but is included here to aid reading\n         * the RX buffer.\n         * This is a good place to put a breakpoint. Here (after first time through the loop) the local status register will be set for last event\n         * and if a good receive has happened the data buffer will have the data in it, and frame_len will be set to the length of the RX frame. */\n        memset(rx_buffer, 0, sizeof(rx_buffer));\n\n        /* Activate reception immediately. See NOTE 2 below. */\n        dwt_rxenable(DWT_START_RX_IMMEDIATE);\n\n        /* Poll until a frame is properly received or an error/timeout occurs. See NOTE 3 below.\n         * STATUS register is 5 bytes long but, as the event we are looking at is in the first byte of the register, we can use this simplest API\n         * function to access it. */\n        waitforsysstatus(&amp;status_reg, 0, (DWT_INT_RXFCG_BIT_MASK | SYS_STATUS_ALL_RX_ERR), 0);\n\n        if (status_reg &amp; DWT_INT_RXFCG_BIT_MASK)",

    {
      "codeBlock": {
        "relativeWorkspacePath": ".\\Src\\examples\\shared_data\\shared_functions.c",
        "range": {
          "startPosition": {
            "line": 552,
            "column": 1
          },
          "endPosition": {
            "line": 590,
            "column": 31
          }
        },
        "contents": "/*! ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------\n * @brief This function will continuously read the system status register until it matches the bits set in the mask\n *        input parameter. It will then exit the function.\n *        This is useful to use when waiting on particular events to occurs. For example, the user could wait for a\n *        good UWB frame to be received and/or no receive errors have occurred.\n *        The lower 32-bits of the system status register will be read in a while loop. Each iteration of the loop will check if a matching\n *        mask value for the higher 32-bits of the system status register is set. If the mask value is set in the higher 32-bits of the system\n *        status register, the function will return that value along with the last recorded value of the lower 32-bits of the system status\n *        register. Thus, the user should be aware that this function will not wait for high and low mask values to be set in both the low and high\n *        system status registers. Alternatively, the user can call this function to *only* check the higher or lower system status registers.\n *\n * input parameters\n * @param lo_result - A pointer to a uint32_t that will contain the final value of the system status register (lower 32 bits).\n *                    Pass in a NULL pointer to ignore returning this value.\n * @param hi_result - A pointer to a uint32_t that will contain the final value of the system status register (higher 32 bits).\n *                    Pass in a NULL pointer to ignore returning this value.\n * @param lo_mask - a uint32 mask value that is used to check for certain bits to be set in the system status register (lower 32 bits).\n *               Example values to use are as follows:\n *               DWT_INT_TXFRS_BIT_MASK - Wait for a TX frame to be sent.\n *               SYS_STATUS_RXFCG_BIT_MASK | SYS_STATUS_ALL_RX_ERR - Wait for frame to be received and no reception errors.\n *               SYS_STATUS_RXFCG_BIT_MASK | SYS_STATUS_ALL_RX_TO | SYS_STATUS_ALL_RX_ERR - Wait for frame to be received and no receive timeout errors\n *                                                                                          and no reception errors.\n *               SYS_STATUS_RXFR_BIT_MASK | SYS_STATUS_ALL_RX_TO | SYS_STATUS_ALL_ND_RX_ERR - Wait for packet to be received and no receive timeout errors\n *                                                                                            and no reception errors.\n *                                                                                            These flags are useful when polling for STS Mode 4 (no data)\n *                                                                                            packets.\n *               0 - The function will not wait for any bits in the system status register (lower 32 bits).\n * @param hi_mask - a uint32 mask value that is used to check for certain bits to be set in the system status register (higher 32 bits).\n *               Example values to use are as follows:\n *               SYS_STATUS_HI_CCA_FAIL_BIT_MASK - Check for CCA fail status.\n *               0 - The function will not wait for any bits in the system status register (lower 32 bits).\n *\n * return None\n */\nvoid waitforsysstatus(uint32_t *lo_result, uint32_t *hi_result, uint32_t lo_mask, uint32_t hi_mask)\n{\n    uint32_t lo_result_tmp = 0;",

        "detailedLines": [
          {
            "text": "/*! ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------",

          {
            "text": " * @brief This function will continuously read the system status register until it matches the bits set in the mask",
            "lineNumber": 556
          },
          {
            "text": " *        input parameter. It will then exit the function.",
            "lineNumber": 557
          },
          {
            "text": " *        This is useful to use when waiting on particular events to occurs. For example, the user could wait for a",
            "lineNumber": 558
          },
          {
            "text": " *        good UWB frame to be received and/or no receive errors have occurred.",
            "lineNumber": 559
          },
          {
            "text": " *        The lower 32-bits of the system status register will be read in a while loop. Each iteration of the loop will check if a matching",
            "lineNumber": 560
          },
          {
            "text": " *        mask value for the higher 32-bits of the system status register is set. If the mask value is set in the higher 32-bits of the system",
            "lineNumber": 561
          },
          {
            "text": " *        status register, the function will return that value along with the last recorded value of the lower 32-bits of the system status",
            "lineNumber": 562
          },
          {
            "text": " *        register. Thus, the user should be aware that this function will not wait for high and low mask values to be set in both the low and high",
            "lineNumber": 563
          },
          {
            "text": " *        system status registers. Alternatively, the user can call this function to *only* check the higher or lower system status registers.",
            "lineNumber": 564
          },
          {
            "text": " *",
            "lineNumber": 565
          },
          {
            "text": " * input parameters",
            "lineNumber": 566
          },
          {
            "text": " * @param lo_result - A pointer to a uint32_t that will contain the final value of the system status register (lower 32 bits).",

          },
          {
            "text": " *                    Pass in a NULL pointer to ignore returning this value.",
            "lineNumber": 568
          },
          {
            "text": " * @param hi_result - A pointer to a uint32_t that will contain the final value of the system status register (higher 32 bits).",
            "lineNumber": 569
          },
          {
            "text": " *                    Pass in a NULL pointer to ignore returning this value.",
            "lineNumber": 570
          },
          {
            "text": " * @param lo_mask - a uint32 mask value that is used to check for certain bits to be set in the system status register (lower 32 bits).",
            "lineNumber": 571
          },
          {

    {
      "codeBlock": {
        "relativeWorkspacePath": ".\\Src\\examples\\ex_05b_ds_twr_resp\\ds_twr_responder_sts.c",
        "range": {

            "line": 365,
            "column": 61
          },
          "endPosition": {
            "line": 522,
            "column": 150
          }
        },
        "contents": "                    /* as DS-TWR initiator is waiting for RNG_DELAY_MS before next poll transmission\n                     * we can add a delay here before RX is re-enabled again\n                     */\n\n                    Sleep(RNG_DELAY_MS - 10); // start couple of ms earlier\n\n                    /*\n                     * It is OK to reset the STS count when the next loop starts.\n                     * We have the last message in the sequence and can start again.\n                     */\n                    messageFlag = 0;\n                }\n                else\n                {\n                    errors[BAD_FRAME_ERR_IDX] += 1;\n                    /*\n                     * If any error occurs, we can reset the STS count back to default value.\n                     */\n                    messageFlag = 0;\n                }\n            }\n            else\n            {\n                errors[RTO_ERR_IDX] += 1;\n                /*\n                 * If any error occurs, we can reset the STS count back to default value.\n                 */\n                messageFlag = 0;\n            }\n        }\n        else\n        {\n            check_for_status_errors(status_reg, errors);\n\n            if (!(status_reg &amp; DWT_INT_RXFCG_BIT_MASK))\n            {\n                errors[BAD_FRAME_ERR_IDX] += 1;\n            }\n            if (goodSts &lt; 0)\n            {\n                errors[PREAMBLE_COUNT_ERR_IDX] += 1;\n            }\n            if (stsQual &lt;= 0)\n            {\n                errors[CP_QUAL_ERR_IDX] += 1;\n            }\n            /* Clear RX error events in the DW IC status register. */\n            dwt_writesysstatuslo(SYS_STATUS_ALL_RX_ERR);\n\n            /*\n             * If any error occurs, we can reset the STS count back to default value.\n             */\n            messageFlag = 0;\n        }\n    }\n    return DWT_SUCCESS;\n}\n#endif\n/*****************************************************************************************************************************************************\n * NOTES:\n *\n * 1. The double-sided two-way ranging scheme implemented here has to be considered carefully as the accuracy of the distance measured is highly\n *    sensitive to the clock offset error between the devices and the length of the response delay between frames. To achieve the best possible\n *    accuracy, this response delay must be kept as low as possible. In order to do so, 6.8 Mbps data rate is advised in this example and the response\n *    delay between frames is defined as low as possible. The user is referred to User Manual for more details about the double-sided two-way ranging\n *    process.\n *\n *    Initiator: |Poll TX| ..... |Resp RX| ........ |Final TX|\n *    Responder: |Poll RX| ..... |Resp TX| ........ |Final RX|\n *                   ^|P RMARKER|                                    - time of Poll TX/RX\n *                                   ^|R RMARKER|                    - time of Resp TX/RX\n *                                                      ^|R RMARKER| - time of Final TX/RX\n *\n *                       &lt;--TDLY-&gt;                                   - POLL_TX_TO_RESP_RX_DLY_UUS (RDLY-RLEN)\n *                               &lt;-RLEN-&gt;                            - RESP_RX_TIMEOUT_UUS   (length of poll frame)\n *                    &lt;----RDLY------&gt;                               - POLL_RX_TO_RESP_TX_DLY_UUS (depends on how quickly responder\n *                                                                                                                      can turn around and reply)\n *\n *\n *                                        &lt;--T2DLY-&gt;                 - RESP_TX_TO_FINAL_RX_DLY_UUS (R2DLY-FLEN)\n *                                                  &lt;-FLEN---&gt;       - FINAL_RX_TIMEOUT_UUS   (length of response frame)\n *                                    &lt;----RDLY---------&gt;            - RESP_RX_TO_FINAL_TX_DLY_UUS (depends on how quickly initiator\n *                                                                                                                      can turn around and reply)\n *\n *\n * 2. The sum of the values is the TX to RX antenna delay, experimentally determined by a calibration process. Here we use a hard coded typical value\n *    but, in a real application, each device should have its own antenna delay properly calibrated to get the best possible precision when performing\n *    range measurements.\n * 3. The frames used here are Decawave specific ranging frames, complying with the IEEE 802.15.4 standard data frame encoding. The frames are the\n *    following:\n *     - a poll message sent by the initiator to trigger the ranging exchange.\n *     - a response message sent by the responder to complete the exchange and provide all information needed by the initiator to compute the\n *       time-of-flight (distance) estimate.\n *    The first 10 bytes of those frame are common and are composed of the following fields:\n *     - byte 0/1: frame control (0x8841 to indicate a data frame using 16-bit addressing).\n *     - byte 2: sequence number, incremented for each new frame.\n *     - byte 3/4: PAN ID (0xDECA).\n *     - byte 5/6: destination address, see NOTE 4 below.\n *     - byte 7/8: source address, see NOTE 4 below.\n *     - byte 9: function code (specific values to indicate which message it is in the ranging process).\n *    The remaining bytes are specific to each message as follows:\n *    Poll message:\n *     - no more data\n *    Response message:\n *     - byte 10 -&gt; 13: poll message reception timestamp.\n *     - byte 14 -&gt; 17: response message transmission timestamp.\n *    All messages end with a 2-byte checksum automatically set by DW IC.\n * 4. Source and destination addresses are hard coded constants in this example to keep it simple but for a real product every device should have a\n *    unique ID. Here, 16-bit addressing is used to keep the messages as short as possible but, in an actual application, this should be done only\n *    after an exchange of specific messages used to define those short addresses for each device participating to the ranging exchange.\n * 5. In a real application, for optimum performance within regulatory limits, it may be necessary to set TX pulse bandwidth and TX power, (using\n *    the dwt_configuretxrf API call) to per device calibrated values saved in the target system or the DW IC OTP memory.\n * 6. We use polled mode of operation here to keep the example as simple as possible but all status events can be used to generate interrupts. Please\n *    refer to DW IC User Manual for more details on \"interrupts\". It is also to be noted that STATUS register is 5 bytes long but, as the event we\n *    use are all in the first bytes of the register, we can use the simple dwt_read32bitreg() API call to access it instead of reading the whole 5\n *    bytes.\n * 7. As we want to send final TX timestamp in the final message, we have to compute it in advance instead of relying on the reading of DW IC\n *    register. Timestamps and delayed transmission time are both expressed in device time units so we just have to add the desired response delay to\n *    response RX timestamp to get final transmission time. The delayed transmission time resolution is 512 device time units which means that the\n *    lower 9 bits of the obtained value must be zeroed. This also allows to encode the 40-bit value in a 32-bit words by shifting the all-zero lower\n *    8 bits.\n * 8. In this operation, the high order byte of each 40-bit timestamps is discarded. This is acceptable as those time-stamps are not separated by\n *    more than 2**32 device time units (which is around 67 ms) which means that the calculation of the round-trip delays (needed in the\n *    time-of-flight computation) can be handled by a 32-bit subtraction.\n * 9. dwt_writetxdata() takes the full size of the message as a parameter but only copies (size - 2) bytes as the check-sum at the end of the frame is\n *    automatically appended by the DW IC. This means that our variable could be two bytes shorter without losing any data (but the sizeof would not\n *    work anymore then as we would still have to indicate the full length of the frame to dwt_writetxdata()).\n * 10. When running this example on the Dw3000 eval board platform with the POLL_RX_TO_RESP_TX_DLY response delay provided, the dwt_starttx() is always\n *     successful. However, in cases where the delay is too short (or something else interrupts the code flow), then the dwt_starttx() might be issued\n *     too late for the configured start time. The code below provides an example of how to handle this condition: In this case it abandons the\n *     ranging exchange and simply goes back to awaiting another poll message. If this error handling code was not here, a late dwt_starttx() would\n *     result in the code flow getting stuck waiting subsequent RX event that will will never come. The companion \"initiator\" example (ex_06a) should\n *     timeout from awaiting the \"response\" and proceed to send another poll in due course to initiate another ranging exchange.\n * 11. The user is referred to DecaRanging ARM application (distributed with EVK1000 product) for additional practical example of usage, and to the\n *     DW IC API Guide for more details on the DW IC driver functions.\n * 12. In this example, the DW IC is put into IDLE state after calling dwt_initialise(). This means that a fast SPI rate of up to 20 MHz can be used\n *     thereafter.\n * 13. This example uses STS with a packet configuration of mode 1 which looks like so:\n *    ---------------------------------------------------\n *    | Ipatov Preamble | SFD | STS | PHR | PHY Payload |\n *    ---------------------------------------------------\n *    There is a possibility that the TX and RX units in this example will go out of sync as their STS IV values may be misaligned. The STS IV value\n *    changes upon each receiving and transmitting event by the chip. While the TX and RX devices in this example start at the same STS IV values, it\n *    is possible that they can go out sync if a signal is not received correctly, devices are out of range, etc. To combat this, the 'poll message'\n *    that the initiator sends to the responder contains a plain-text STS counter value. The responder receives this message and first checks if\n *    the received frame is out of sync with it's own counter. If so, it will use this received counter value to update it's own counter. When out\n *    of sync with each other, the STS will not align correctly - thus we get no secure timestamp values.\n * 14. Desired configuration by user may be different to the current programmed configuration. dwt_configure is called to set desired\n *     configuration.\n * 15. In this operation, the high order byte of each 40-bit timestamps is discarded. This is acceptable as those time-stamps are not separated by\n *     more than 2**32 device time units (which is around 67 ms) which means that the calculation of the round-trip delays (needed in the\n *     time-of-flight computation) can be handled by a 32-bit subtraction.\n * 16. This example will set the STS key and IV upon each iteration of the main while loop. While this has the benefit of keeping the STS count in\n *     sync with the responder device (which does the same), it should be noted that this is not a 'secure' implementation as the count is reset upon\n *     each iteration of the loop. An attacker could potentially recognise this pattern if the signal was being monitored. While it serves it's\n *     purpose in this simple example, it should not be utilised in any final solution.\n ****************************************************************************************************************************************************/",

            "text": " * 1. The double-sided two-way ranging scheme implemented here has to be considered carefully as the accuracy of the distance measured is highly",

            "lineNumber": 429

            "lineNumber": 430

            "lineNumber": 431

            "lineNumber": 432

          {

            "text": " *     configuration.",

          },

            "text": " * 15. In this operation, the high order byte of each 40-bit timestamps is discarded. This is acceptable as those time-stamps are not separated by",
            "lineNumber": 516
